clue.text: Draw attention to employees somewhere in Arizona

parts.note: to flag something is to draw attention to it
a firm's staff are its employees

explanation.surface: A manager tries to get noticed by the workforce at some Arizona site.
explanation.definitionFit: Flagstaff is a city in northern Arizona, so it is a place somewhere in that state.

clue.text: Police officer's to pay for accommodation, initially

indicators.note: initially says the word for accommodation comes first, before the word for paying

parts.note: a flat is accommodation
to foot the bill is to pay for it

explanation.surface: A policeman must pay for his lodgings at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' is not a first-letter signal here: it puts the accommodation ahead of the payment, against the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: Flatfoot is an old slang term for a policeman on the beat.

clue.text: Tony, for example, is first-rate attraction? The reverse

parts.note: A means first-rate, as in A1 or an A grade

indicators.note: the reverse tells us to turn the word for attraction backwards

parts.note: a draw is an attraction that pulls in crowds

explanation.surface: Is a Tony a top draw, or is it the other way round?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tony' is the Broadway theatre prize, not a man's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A Tony is a prize given for Broadway theatre, so it is one example of a prize.

clue.text: Film recaptures exotic break

indicators.note: exotic suggests the letters of the words become something strange and foreign

explanation.surface: A movie recreates a holiday in some far-off place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'break' looks like a holiday, but it is a broken bone.
explanation.definitionFit: A simple fracture is a bone break where the skin is not pierced.

clue.text: Stand near the chimney and do some housework

parts.note: to iron is to do some household chores

explanation.surface: Stand by the fireplace and get on with the chores.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stand' looks like a verb but is a noun, a support in the fireplace.
explanation.definitionFit: Andirons are metal supports for logs in a hearth, a stand by the chimney.

clue.text: Corrupt police? Constable's work they might enhance

explanation.surface: Bent coppers might boost a constable's paperwork.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constable' is the painter John Constable, not a policeman: picture framers display paintings well; corrupt police frame suspects.
explanation.definitionFit: Crooked officers who plant evidence frame people, and picture framers mount paintings such as Constable's landscapes.

clue.text: Swindle naughty kid out of a penny

indicators.note: out of says the penny's letter is taken away from the word for the child

parts.note: a scamp is a mischievous child
P is the abbreviation for a penny

explanation.surface: A con trick in which a mischievous child is cheated of a coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A scam is a fraudulent scheme, a synonym of swindle as a noun.

clue.text: Musical style upset the Spanish in Madrid bar

indicators.note: in places the turned article inside the word for the bar

parts.note: a cantina is a bar in Spanish-speaking places

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the word is turned backwards

parts.note: el is the Spanish for the

explanation.surface: A style of music annoyed the Spaniards in a bar in Madrid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns the Spanish article to LE; 'in' sets it inside the bar. A cantina is a Spanish-style bar.
explanation.definitionFit: A cantilena is a smooth lyrical vocal melody or style of writing.

clue.text: I'm up on fashion? It's an illusion

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the letters read from the bottom upward

parts.note: taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe
a rage is a fashion or craze

explanation.surface: Someone thinks they are trendy, but it is all in the mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns IM into MI; 'on' places it above RAGE in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is an optical illusion, something seen that is not there.

clue.text: Bossy types create it with heretics

parts.note: to author is to create
Arians followed the heresy of Arius about the nature of Christ

explanation.surface: Domineering people stir up trouble alongside heretics.
explanation.definitionFit: Authoritarians demand obedience, so they are domineering people.

clue.text: Flap like wings and tail of bantam

parts.note: alar is an adjective meaning relating to or like wings

indicators.note: tail of picks the final letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A bantam hen flutters its wings and tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flap' looks like a verb about wings, but here it is the noun for a state of panic.
explanation.definitionFit: A flap is a state of agitation or panic, the same as alarm.

clue.text: Take off as party with one candidate?

parts.note: a do is a party
a means one
a runner is a candidate in a race or contest

explanation.surface: An election with only one contender, treated as a celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: DO A RUNNER is British slang for running off, especially without paying.
explanation.definitionFit: To do a runner is slang for leaving in a hurry, often to escape a bill, so it means to bolt.

clue.text: Roof-top rogue?

parts.note: points to the musical about a violinist on the roof, and to a word for a cheat or swindler

explanation.surface: A burglar or prowler up among the chimneys.
explanation.walkthrough: The roof-top points to the musical Fiddler on the Roof; a fiddler is also someone who fiddles accounts, a rogue.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiddler is a cheat, and in the famous show the violinist plays on a roof.

clue.text: Reproducing sound of group singing mostly in English

indicators.note: in places the shortened word for the singers inside the abbreviation for English
mostly says the last letter of the word for the singers is dropped

parts.note: a choir is a group of singers

explanation.surface: A recording of an English choir.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' drops the choir's last letter; 'in' sets what is left inside the English abbreviation. 'Reproducing sound' is the definition, not a homophone signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Something echoing repeats a sound back, reproducing it.

clue.text: Nuts, and where to pick them, if home-grown

definitions.text: where to pick them, if home-grown

explanation.surface: Advice on harvesting nuts from your own garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' first means crazy; the second reading imagines picking home-grown nuts from your own tree.
explanation.definitionFit: Out of one's tree is slang for crazy, and home-grown fruit or nuts come from a tree one owns.

clue.text: Two birds circling counter in old tax building

parts.note: a tit is a small bird

indicators.note: circling means the second bird goes around the counter

parts.note: a hen is a bird
a bar is a counter where drinks are served

explanation.surface: A pair of birds fly around a shop counter in an ancient tax office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two birds' supplies both TIT and HEN; 'circling' wraps the second bird around the counter. A tithe was a tenth of produce owed to the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A tithe barn stored the tenth of produce paid as a church levy, so it is a building tied to an old tax.

clue.text: Wagered a couple of blokes behaved perfidiously

parts.note: bet means wagered
Ray is a man's name
Ed is a man's name

explanation.surface: Two men placed a bet and then double-crossed each other.
explanation.definitionFit: To have betrayed someone is to have acted treacherously, which is what perfidious means.

clue.text: Cooked pecan tarts for roadside eatery

indicators.note: cooked suggests the letters of the words are worked over into a new form

explanation.surface: Pecan tarts were baked to sell at a café by the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' looks like a link word but is part of the fodder: PECANTARTS plus FOR gives the thirteen letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A transport café is a British roadside diner used chiefly by lorry drivers.

clue.text: Lad from Bangladesh arranged operation

indicators.note: arranged means the remaining letters are put in a new order
from says the young man's letters are taken out of the country's name

explanation.surface: A boy from Bangladesh set up a surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' removes LAD from BANGLADESH, leaving BANGESH, which 'arranged' reorders.
explanation.definitionFit: A shebang, as in the whole shebang, is an affair or business set-up.

clue.text: Showing no inclination for strike? That's odd

parts.note: to be off something is to have lost one's liking for it
to beat is to strike

explanation.surface: Someone who does not want to go on strike is thought peculiar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'strike' suggests industrial action, but it is the verb hit.
explanation.definitionFit: Offbeat means unconventional or eccentric, a synonym of odd.

clue.text: Secret policemen's period of inactivity

explanation.surface: The secret police are having a quiet spell.
explanation.walkthrough: The Stasi was East Germany's secret police; with an apostrophe-s it reads as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The Stasi was the East German secret police, and stasis is a state of stagnation or standstill.

clue.text: A thespian, primarily, is seen in that place

definitions.text: A thespian, primarily, is seen in that place

indicators.note: is seen in says the article and the actor's initial go inside the word for that place

parts.note: there means in that place

indicators.note: primarily picks the opening letter of the word that follows

explanation.surface: Where an actor is chiefly to be found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is seen in' puts A plus T (first of 'thespian') inside THERE; the whole clue also describes where an actor is seen.
explanation.definitionFit: A playhouse is the venue where actors are seen performing.

clue.text: Author borrowed from Woolf or Sterne?

indicators.note: borrowed from says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: Which novelist took his ideas from Virginia Woolf or Laurence Sterne?
explanation.walkthrough: The run sits across 'WoolF OR STERne'.
explanation.definitionFit: E. M. Forster was an English novelist, so he is an author.

clue.text: Ex-BBC man brought up English family

indicators.note: brought up in a down clue means the name is read from the bottom upward

parts.note: John Birt was a former Director-General of the BBC

explanation.surface: A former BBC boss raised an English household.
explanation.walkthrough: John Birt ran the BBC in the 1990s.
explanation.definitionFit: A tribe is a group of related families or a clan, a kind of extended family.

clue.text: Commotion about a piece of luggage after flight etc.

indicators.note: about says the word for commotion goes around the article

parts.note: a stir is a commotion
a case is a suitcase, a piece of luggage

explanation.surface: Fuss over a lost suitcase after a plane journey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flight' looks like air travel, but a flight of stairs is a staircase.
explanation.definitionFit: A flight of steps, with its handrails and so on, makes up a stairway.

clue.text: Little woman accepts it in friendly spirit

indicators.note: accepts means the name takes in the other word

parts.note: Amy is one of the March sisters in Little Women

explanation.surface: A small lady takes something in good heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' refers to Amy March of Louisa May Alcott's Little Women.
explanation.definitionFit: Amity is friendship or goodwill, a friendly spirit between people.

clue.text: One writer among thousands

indicators.note: among says the name sits inside the letters of the word that follows

explanation.surface: A single author lost in a vast crowd of authors.
explanation.walkthrough: The name sits inside 'thouSANDs'; George Sand was the pen name of a French novelist.
explanation.definitionFit: George Sand was a nineteenth-century French novelist, so a single author.

clue.text: Software expert meeting boss in town

parts.note: Bill Gates founded the software company Microsoft
a head is the boss of an organisation

explanation.surface: A tech mogul meets a chief somewhere in a town.
explanation.walkthrough: GATESHEAD is a town in north-east England, across the Tyne from Newcastle.
explanation.definitionFit: Gateshead is a town in Tyne and Wear in north-east England.
